name: Yusuf Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Yusuf, I'm 27, and I've been a junior copywriter in the marketing team at Brightfield, a snack brand that makes crisps and oat bars, for about a year and a half. I live with my partner Hana, who's a nurse on a children's ward, in a rented flat above a laundrette. I did English at university and kind of fell into marketing because it was the job that actually paid for writing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get in around nine, check what Claire, my manager, has dropped into the shared tracker, and then it's mostly writing: social posts, the back-of-pack blurbs, the monthly email. I like finding the one line that makes a bag of crisps sound like a small treat instead of a bag of crisps. What wears me out is the rounds of changes, where legal, sales and Claire all want different words and I'm the one stitching it together at six o'clock. I'm honestly still slow at it, and everyone else in the team uses those AI writing tools, but I never have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably post something smug, to be honest, like 'turns out you still need a person to write a joke about cheese and onion.' At work I'd say it out loud at lunch, because people have been teasing me for refusing to use the tools. I'd say good, now can we talk about pay instead of robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't fix my real problem, which is that I'm the slowest writer in a team of six. Even a bit of automation hits the routine stuff first, the product listings and the alt text, and that's half of what a junior like me gets given. So I'd still be quietly worried about my review in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep writing the way I do, but I'd ask Claire for proper feedback every month so my review isn't a surprise. I'd put another 100 a month into savings, because we've only got about three months of rent and bills put by. And I'd finally join the creative workers' union my friend Tunde keeps sending me links about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like relief with a small knot still in it. The world doesn't change, but I'm still the junior who takes twice as long, and the rent on the flat went up again in September. I'd sleep better than I do now, but not perfectly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said even a little automation takes the routine stuff. What exactly would go first from your week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The product listings for the supermarket websites, easily. There are about forty of them every time we change a pack, and the others already do theirs with a tool in an afternoon while I take two days. If the listings go, my week has a big hole in it, and my manager will notice the hole before she notices my good lines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Hana say if you came home worried about that review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hana would tell me to just learn the tool and stop being stubborn, because that's what she says about everything with a screen. I'd tell her my job is the writing, not the button, and then we'd argue about it while making dinner. She's probably right, which is the annoying part.

say: I'd joke that you still need a **person** to write a crisp joke, and say good riddance to the hype.
I'd tell the team we should talk about **pay**, not robots, now the scare is over.
think: I'm still the **slowest writer** in a team of six, and that hasn't changed.
Even small automation takes the **product listings**, which fill half of a junior's week.
do: Ask Claire for **monthly feedback** so the March review isn't a surprise.
Put an **extra 100** a month into savings on top of the three months already there.
Join the **creative workers' union** that his friend Tunde keeps recommending.
feel: **Relief** that the world stays the same, with a small knot about his own slow pace.
Still uneasy because the **rent** went up again in September.
S0.quote: If the listings go, my week has a big hole in it, and my manager will notice the hole before she notices my good lines.
fieldNote: He treats refusing AI as a **point of principle**, and the team teases him for it.
His real worry is **being slow**, which no plateau fixes.

steps.text: Ask Claire for written feedback on his copy every month before the March review
Move an extra 100 a month into the savings account
Join the creative workers' union his friend Tunde recommended

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: this is a choice companies are making, not the weather. Online I'd share stuff about writers losing work and say the brands should have to label AI copy. At work I'd push for us to talk to HR about what happens to juniors before it happens, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it means I'm first out. If software is writing the listings, the emails and the first drafts, then the person they need is someone who checks and edits, and Claire would pick Priya, who's quick and already uses all of it. I'm the obvious cut in a team of six, and I know it. My manager would keep my quickest colleague, who already uses every AI tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start applying for jobs that are more face to face, like events or community work for a charity, maybe in the first three months. I'd move our savings up from three months to five by skipping the trip to Hana's family in the spring. And I'd get the union involved early, because I want someone in the room when they decide who goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like the feeling when you see your name on a meeting invite with HR and no subject line. I'm angry at the companies selling this stuff, but I'm also scared, and those two feelings don't sit well together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're sure you'd be the one to go. Have you thought about learning the tools, the way Priya has?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I've thought about it, and I keep not doing it. Part of it's principle, because I don't want to train the thing that replaces people like me. Part of it is just that I'm slow with new software and I'm embarrassed to be bad at it in front of everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you did lose the job, how long could you and Hana manage on what you have?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hana's pay covers the rent, just about, so we wouldn't be on the street. But the three months of savings is my half of everything else, the bills, the phone, the car insurance. After about four months we'd be eating into what we were saving for a deposit, and that dream would be gone.

say: I'd say job cuts are a **choice companies make**, not the weather.
I'd argue brands should have to **label AI copy** and talk to juniors before cutting.
think: I'm the **obvious cut** in a team of six, because I'm slow and don't use AI.
Claire would keep **Priya**, who's quicker and already uses every tool.
do: Apply for **face-to-face jobs** like charity events within the first three months.
Grow savings from three to **five months** by skipping the spring trip to Hana's family.
Bring the **union** in early so someone is there when cuts are decided.
feel: **Sick and angry**, like an HR meeting invite with no subject line.
Embarrassed that he's **avoided learning** the tools out of principle and pride.
S1.quote: I'm the obvious cut in a team of six, and I know it. My manager would keep my quickest colleague, who already uses every AI tool.
fieldNote: He openly expects to be **first out**, while still refusing to try the tools.

steps.text: Apply for charity events and community jobs within three months
Skip the spring trip to Hana's family and bank the money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it, honestly. I'd be posting about a pause, about taxing the companies that do this, about some kind of basic income. At work I'd say the whole team should go to the union together, not one by one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my career is over before it really started. Writing copy is pure thinking work, there's nothing hands-on about it, so 2028 is my date. Robots coming three years later doesn't help me, except that maybe I could go and do something with my hands until 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd stop the deposit savings and turn them into a just-in-case fund. I'd look into a care job or a warehouse job, anything physical, because that buys me those three years. And I'd go to every union meeting and every protest about it, because a law is the only thing that would actually help someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor just went. Two years isn't enough time to retrain into anything real, and I'm not someone who changes quickly. I keep thinking about Hana working nights while I try to figure out who I am if I'm not a writer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a care job. Would you actually do that, or is it just an idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I would, because my mum was a care worker and I used to help her on weekends when I was a teenager. It's hard work and the pay is bad, but nobody's going to want a robot giving their nan a bath in 2029, so care work buys me time. It's not what I studied for, though, and that stings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Hana's job? Does she feel safe in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hana thinks nurses are fine, and maybe for a few years they are, because it's hands-on. But if the robots come in 2031, then we're both on a clock, just different clocks. That's the part I can't get out of my head at three in the morning.

say: I'd call for a **pause**, a tax on AI firms, and a **basic income**.
I'd tell the team to go to the **union together**, not one by one.
think: Copy is pure thinking work, so **2028** is the date his career ends.
Robots arriving in 2031 only matter because **hands-on work** buys him three years.

Apply for **care or warehouse work** to buy three years before robots arrive.

feel: Like the **floor went**, with no time to retrain into anything real.

S2.quote: Nobody's going to want a robot giving their nan a bath in 2029, so care work buys me time.
fieldNote: He sees the **three-year gap** as a refuge in hands-on care work.
His mum's **care work** makes that fallback feel real rather than abstract.
He believes only **politics and law** can help someone who changes slowly.

steps.text: Move the house deposit savings into an emergency fund in the first month
Apply for care worker jobs like the ones his mum did
Attend union meetings and protests calling for an AI law
Vote and campaign for a tax on AI firms and a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really, but with more time to organise. I'd say we have five years to get rules in place, so let's not waste them. I'd want writers and designers to have a proper voice, maybe a guild like actors have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to watch it coming, which might be worse. I'd be 32 when it lands, and I'd have spent five years in a job I knew was ending. I think I'd still be the one who drags his feet, and that's what worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give myself one year to pick a direction, probably nursing like Hana or something in social care, and start an access course by the second year. I'd keep the copy job as long as it pays. And we'd keep saving for the deposit, but we'd go for a cheaper place in the town where Hana grew up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, but not frantic. Five years means there's time to be sensible, which means there's time to make the wrong choice slowly. I'd want someone to just tell me what to retrain in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why nursing, if you'd said care work for the fast version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with five years I could actually get qualified, instead of just grabbing any job. And nursing has three extra years before robots on top of that, so maybe eight years of real work. Hana says I'd hate the shifts, and she'd know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move to Hana's hometown. What's pulling you there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Houses there cost about half what they do here, and her parents are ten minutes away. If we're both retraining or juggling shifts, having her mum around matters. I'd miss the city, but I wouldn't miss the rent.

I'd push for a **guild** for writers and designers, like actors have.

Start an **access course** by the second year while keeping the copy job.
Buy a cheaper home in **Hana's hometown**, where houses cost about half.

S3.quote: Five years means there's time to be sensible, which means there's time to make the wrong choice slowly.
fieldNote: More time makes him **plan**, but he still expects to stall.
Nursing appeals because **hands-on work** adds three years after AGI.
Family support from **Hana's parents** shapes where they'd live.

steps.text: Choose between nursing and social care within the first year
Enrol on a nursing access course by the second year
Buy a cheaper flat near Hana's parents in her hometown
Push for a writers' and designers' guild through the union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so governments have no excuse. I'd post about free retraining for anyone in a desk job. And at work I'd try to get the company to fund courses for juniors now, not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is the first version where I think I'd be okay. I'd be 37, and if I start something new by 30 I'd have a real career by then. Honestly the copy job would probably shrink well before 2036 anyway, so the clock starts sooner than the card says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep writing at Brightfield for a few more years while I train part-time, probably as a nurse. We'd buy the place near Hana's parents in about three years. I'd also join the union now and help write what we want, because ten years is long enough for a campaign to win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but not calm. I can see a road, but I'm someone who doesn't like change, and this is ten years of change. Mostly I feel like I'd want to get started and stop dreading it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the copy job would shrink before 2036. How soon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably within three or four years, the way the others already work faster with tools. By 2030 I think the snack brand I work for might have two writers instead of six. So I'd want to be halfway through training by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had children by then, would that change the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about kids around 31 or 32, so yes, it would. I wouldn't want to be in college with a baby and no proper income. That's another reason to start training early and not wait for 2036.

S4.quote: By 2030 I think the snack brand I work for might have two writers instead of six.
fieldNote: He expects the **real clock** to start years before the card's date.
**Children** around 31 make him want to train early.

steps.text: Train part-time as a nurse while keeping the Brightfield job
Buy a home near Hana's parents in about three years
Help draft the union's demands on AI and retraining
Plan children for after the nursing course, around age 32

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because there's no time for someone like me who changes slowly. What would help is free retraining with a wage while you do it, so I could become a nurse without us losing the flat. And a union that actually gets a seat at the table.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'm ashamed of not using the tools. I tell everyone refusing the AI tools is principle, and it is, but some of it is fear of looking stupid. I'd rather be honest about that.

headlineQuote: I tell everyone refusing the AI tools is principle, and it is, but some of it is fear of looking stupid.
portrait: Yusuf is a **27-year-old junior copywriter** at a snack brand, living with Hana, a nurse.
He refuses to use **AI tools** on principle, and partly from fear of looking slow.
He expects to be the **first cut** in his team once AI spreads.
In the fast AGI picture he'd fall back on **care work**, like his mum did.
With more time he plans to **retrain as a nurse** and move near Hana's parents.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he changes slowly and two years leaves no time.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** so he could become a nurse without losing the flat.
A **union** with a real seat at the table.
